newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Asian shares end mixed after baht float.
newsitem.headline: Asian shares end mixed after baht float.

text.p: Thailand's stock market resoundingly cheered Wednesday's baht flotation but reactions were mixed across other Asian bourses.

The Thai stock market initially dropped 1.1 percent on news the Thai exchange rate system would be changed to a managed float instead of set against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
But the turnaround was swift, and the composite SET stock index finished the day up 41.51 points, or 7.87 percent, to 568.79.

"There was a tremendous buildup of funds that were waiting to go into the market if there was a devaluation or, as it happened, a flotation," George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett, told Reuters Financial Television.
Rumours had been swirling in the markets for months that the baht may be devalued against the backdrop of the slowest economic growth in Thailand in a decade.
Thailand's neighbours, which have sometimes suffered as Thai economic fortunes ebbed, showed disparate responses to Wednesday's baht news.
Malaysia's Composite Index of 100 blue chips gained 5.98 points, or 0.55 percent, to close at 1,084.88 after shrugging off the Thai news and rising instead on local retail and institutional buying.
On the other hand, the Philippines' composite index closed down 1.8 percent at 2,764.89 as wild swings in the foreign exchange market spooked investors.

Earlier in the day, the Philippine Central Bank offered one-day reverse repos at 20 percent and later raised them to 24 percent to curb a speculative attack on the peso. It also sold millions of dollars to defend the local currency after Thailand's baht announcement.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrials Index ended down 12.37 points, or 0.62 percent, to 1,968.91.
Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, the Jakarta Composite Index edged down 1.464 points, or 0.20 percent, to 730.155 after hitting a record high of 734.02 earlier in the day.
Other regional markets that posted gains did so on the back of domestic factors.
South Korean shares closed up 2.54 percent, or 19.26 points, to 777.29 on broad optimism about an economic recovery.
Australian stocks notched a record close, with the All Ordinaries Index leaping 24.7 points to end at 2,745.9 on continued bullish momentum.
In Tokyo, shares added 20.90 points, or 0.10 percent, to close at 20,196.42, helped in part by bargain-hunting, brokers said.
Hong Kong's stock market was closed for a three-day holiday marking the territory's return to Chinese rule. It is expected to rally when it reopens on Thursday.
The Bombay index was up 39.39 points, or 0.92 percent, to 4,340.25 at 0931 GMT, helped by foreign fund and local buying.
Elsewhere in Asia, Shanghai's foreign currency B shares closed down 3.42 percent to 78.690, while in Taiwan, the key stock index sank 33.56 points, or 0.37 percent, to 8,996.72.
Several analysts said they remain watchful on Thailand despite the relief offered by the baht action.
"Their financial system is still very vulnerable to a dramatic shock," said Lum Chee Soon, general manager for group economic research at PhileoAllied Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
